claim: Drosophila melanogaster males deposit the pheromone 9-tricosene upon stimulation with apple cider vinegar food odor.
source: Using Drosophila melanogaster as an animal model, we found that males deposit the pheromone 9-tricosene upon stimulation with the food-odor apple cider vinegar.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from GC-MS analysis showing enrichment of 9-tricosene in apple cider vinegar-stimulated conditions (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 1) and behavioral assays demonstrating male-specific pheromone deposition (Figure 1I).

claim: 9-tricosene acts as a potent aggregation pheromone for both male and female Drosophila.
source: This pheromone acts as a potent aggregation pheromone and as an oviposition guidance cue for females.
evidence: Behavioral data show that 9-tricosene elicits attraction behaviors (Figure 3D-E) and post-stimulus aggregation (Figure 5D,E), and that the aggregation pheromone is equally attractive to both virgin and mated males and females (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).

claim: 9-tricosene functions as an oviposition guidance cue for female Drosophila.
source: This pheromone acts as a potent aggregation pheromone and as an oviposition guidance cue for females.
evidence: Experimental data demonstrate that females laid five-fold more eggs in the pheromone quadrant (Figure 6A′) and significantly more eggs in locations containing 9-tricosene (Figure 6B′).

claim: 9-tricosene activates antennal basiconic Or7a receptors.
source: We use genetic, molecular, electrophysiological, and behavioral approaches to show that 9-tricosene activates antennal basiconic Or7a receptors, a receptor activated by many alcohols and aldehydes such as the green leaf volatile E2-hexenal.
evidence: Single sensillum recordings show that 9-tricosene elicits rapid and robust firing patterns in the antennal basiconic ab4 sensillum expressing Or7a (Figure 4C), and misexpression of Or7a in ab3A neurons endows them the ability to respond to 9-tricosene (Figure 4D,E).

claim: Or7a is a receptor activated by many alcohols and aldehydes including E2-hexenal.
source: We use genetic, molecular, electrophysiological, and behavioral approaches to show that 9-tricosene activates antennal basiconic Or7a receptors, a receptor activated by many alcohols and aldehydes such as the green leaf volatile E2-hexenal.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous comprehensive SSR surveys identifying multiple ligands for Or7a (Hallem and Carlson, 2006), with E2-hexenal identified as the most potent ligand.

claim: Loss of Or7a positive neurons abolishes aggregation behavior towards 9-tricosene.
source: We demonstrate that loss of Or7a positive neurons or the Or7a receptor abolishes aggregation behavior and oviposition site-selection towards 9-tricosene and E2-hexenal.
evidence: Behavioral data show that aggregation responses to both naturally deposited pheromone and 9-tricosene were completely abolished in Or7a neuron-ablated flies (Figure 5B-E) and Or7a mutants (Figure 5B-E).

claim: Loss of Or7a receptor abolishes aggregation behavior towards 9-tricosene.
source: We demonstrate that loss of Or7a positive neurons or the Or7a receptor abolishes aggregation behavior and oviposition site-selection towards 9-tricosene and E2-hexenal.
evidence: Or7a mutants completely lacked attraction to the naturally deposited food-odor-induced pheromone and to 9-tricosene (Figure 5B-E).

claim: Loss of Or7a positive neurons abolishes oviposition site-selection towards 9-tricosene.
source: We demonstrate that loss of Or7a positive neurons or the Or7a receptor abolishes aggregation behavior and oviposition site-selection towards 9-tricosene and E2-hexenal.
evidence: The 9-tricosene guided egg laying preference was abolished when Or7a neurons were ablated (Figure 6C′ and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).

claim: Loss of Or7a receptor abolishes oviposition site-selection towards 9-tricosene.
source: We demonstrate that loss of Or7a positive neurons or the Or7a receptor abolishes aggregation behavior and oviposition site-selection towards 9-tricosene and E2-hexenal.
evidence: The 9-tricosene guided egg laying preference was abolished in Or7a mutant flies (Figure 6D).

claim: Loss of Or7a positive neurons abolishes aggregation behavior towards E2-hexenal.
source: We demonstrate that loss of Or7a positive neurons or the Or7a receptor abolishes aggregation behavior and oviposition site-selection towards 9-tricosene and E2-hexenal.
evidence: E2-hexenal directed Or7a-dependent egg-laying site selection (Figure 7A-D) and attraction (Figure 7E), with Or7a mutants showing abolished responses.

claim: Loss of Or7a receptor abolishes aggregation behavior towards E2-hexenal.
source: We demonstrate that loss of Or7a positive neurons or the Or7a receptor abolishes aggregation behavior and oviposition site-selection towards 9-tricosene and E2-hexenal.
evidence: Or7a mutant flies showed significantly reduced attraction to E2-hexenal compared to wild-type (Figure 7E).

claim: Loss of Or7a positive neurons abolishes oviposition site-selection towards E2-hexenal.
source: We demonstrate that loss of Or7a positive neurons or the Or7a receptor abolishes aggregation behavior and oviposition site-selection towards 9-tricosene and E2-hexenal.
evidence: Egg laying preference of Or7a mutant flies in E2-hexenal assays showed no significant preference (Figure 7D, p=0.68).

claim: Loss of Or7a receptor abolishes oviposition site-selection towards E2-hexenal.
source: We demonstrate that loss of Or7a positive neurons or the Or7a receptor abolishes aggregation behavior and oviposition site-selection towards 9-tricosene and E2-hexenal.
evidence: Or7a mutant flies showed no significant egg-laying preference for E2-hexenal (Figure 7D).

claim: 9-tricosene functions via Or7a to link food-odor perception with aggregation and egg-laying decisions.
source: 9-Tricosene thus functions via Or7a to link food-odor perception with aggregation and egg-laying decisions.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that 9-tricosene is deposited upon food-odor stimulation, activates Or7a receptors, and guides both aggregation and oviposition behaviors in an Or7a-dependent manner.

claim: Flies exhibit robust aggregation to the original odor quadrant for substantial time periods after odor application ceases.
source: During investigations with the food-odor apple cider vinegar, we identified a novel olfactory behavior in which flies showed robust aggregation to the original odor quadrant for substantial time periods subsequent to odor application (Figure 1B,C,G).
evidence: Behavioral tracking data show that flies continued to aggregate in the original odor quadrant after apple cider vinegar was switched to clean air (Figure 1C, Videos 1 and 2), with aggregation persisting for >25 min (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).

claim: Post-stimulus aggregation behavior is not due to residual apple cider vinegar on the glass plates.
source: Perfusion of apple cider vinegar into the empty arena for 5 min in the absence of flies, and introduction of naïve flies into the arena, did not produce post-stimulus aggregation to the original quadrant (Figure 1D), suggesting the post-stimulus aggregation behavior is not due to residual apple cider vinegar on the glass plates.
evidence: Experimental control showing that apple cider vinegar perfusion without flies present did not lead to post-stimulus aggregation when naïve flies were introduced (Figure 1D).

claim: Humidified air attraction does not lead to post-stimulus aggregation behavior.
source: To rule out the possibility of passive pheromone deposition onto the glass plates due to crowding of many flies into a small space, flies were corralled into the odor quadrant by attraction to humidified air and monitored for post-stimulus aggregation behavior. Under these conditions, there was no detectable post-stimulus aggregation (Figure 1E,F, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Behavioral data show that while humidified air was attractive (Figure 1E, left), it did not lead to post-stimulus aggregation (Figure 1E, right; Figure 1F).

claim: Flies may deposit pheromone(s) in specific response to food-odor apple cider vinegar.
source: All together, these data suggest that flies may deposit pheromone(s) in a specific response to the food-odor apple cider vinegar.
evidence: This inference is based on the observation that post-stimulus aggregation occurs after apple cider vinegar but not humidified air stimulation, and not when apple cider vinegar is applied without flies present.

claim: Post-stimulus aggregation behaviors are stimulated by food odors including banana and yeast paste.
source: To determine if post-stimulus aggregation could be induced by other food odors, we tested the food odors banana and yeast paste (Figure 1—figure supplement 7). These stimuli were highly attractive to flies and also induced post-stimulus aggregation.
evidence: Behavioral data show that banana and yeast food odors induced post-stimulus aggregation (Figure 1—figure supplement 7, p < 0.001).

claim: Ethyl acetate, an attractive component of apple cider vinegar, does not generate post-stimulus aggregation behaviors.
source: As a further test, we examined stimulus attraction by a prominent attractive monomolecular odorant of apple cider vinegar: ethyl acetate. Although this odorant was highly attractive, it failed to generate post-stimulus aggregation behaviors (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Behavioral data show ethyl acetate was attractive during stimulus phase but showed no significant post-stimulus aggregation (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).

claim: Post-stimulus aggregation behaviors may be guided specifically by food odors and possibly by food odor perceptions.
source: Together, these data suggest that post-stimulus aggregation behaviors may be guided specifically by food odors, and possibly by food odor perceptions.
evidence: This inference is based on the observation that complex food odors (apple cider vinegar, banana, yeast) induce post-stimulus aggregation while a single attractive component (ethyl acetate) does not.

claim: Male flies are the source of the aggregation pheromone.
source: Only in the presence of male depositor flies did detector flies show post-stimulus aggregation (Figure 1I). This indicates that male flies are the source of the pheromone.
evidence: Behavioral experiments using different combinations of depositor flies (mixed genders, virgin females, or males) showed that only male depositors led to post-stimulus aggregation by detector flies (Figure 1I, p = 0.003).

claim: The aggregation pheromone is equally attractive to both virgin and mated males and females.
source: The aggregation pheromone was equally attractive to both virgin and mated males and females (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: Behavioral data show similar post-stimulus aggregation among virgin males, virgin females, virgin male + virgin females, and premixed males + females (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).

claim: The gustatory system is not necessary for post-stimulus aggregation behavior.
source: Poxn mutants, which exhibit no functional gustatory receptor neurons (Awasaki and Kimura, 2001), were as attracted as wild-type animals (Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1), suggesting that the gustatory system is not necessary for post-stimulus aggregation.
evidence: Behavioral data show that Poxn mutants exhibited similar post-stimulus aggregation to wild-type (Figure 2B, p = 0.2258).

claim: Ppk23 function is not necessary for aggregation behavior.
source: ppk23 mutants exhibited similar post-stimulus aggregation compared to wild-type animals (Figure 2B), suggesting Ppk23 function is not necessary for aggregation and that 7-tricosene is unlikely to be the aggregation pheromone.
evidence: Behavioral data show ppk23 mutants had similar post-stimulus aggregation to wild-type (Figure 2B, p = 0.0951).

claim: 7-tricosene is unlikely to be the aggregation pheromone.
source: ppk23 mutants exhibited similar post-stimulus aggregation compared to wild-type animals (Figure 2B), suggesting Ppk23 function is not necessary for aggregation and that 7-tricosene is unlikely to be the aggregation pheromone.
evidence: This inference is based on the fact that ppk23 is necessary for detection of 7-tricosene (Lu et al., 2012; Thistle et al., 2012), yet ppk23 mutants show normal aggregation behavior.

claim: Most ionotropic receptors are not required for pheromone attraction.
source: The Ir8a and Ir25a double mutant flies exhibited normal post-stimulus aggregation, showing that most ionotropic receptors are not required for the pheromone attraction (Figure 2C).
evidence: Behavioral data show Ir8a/Ir25a double mutants had similar post-stimulus aggregation to wild-type (Figure 2C, p = 0.1524).

claim: In orco mutant flies, attraction behavior to the pheromone was completely abolished and instead repelled by the apple cider vinegar quadrant.
source: Interestingly, in orco mutant flies, attraction behavior to the pheromone was completely abolished and instead repelled by the apple cider vinegar quadrant (Figure 2C).
evidence: Behavioral data show orco mutants exhibited significant repulsion in post-stimulus phase (Figure 2C, p < 0.001).

claim: The repulsion of orco mutants to the apple cider vinegar quadrant is likely due to acid sensing of minimal residual acetic acid mediated by the Ir8a/Ir64a complex.
source: This repulsion is likely due to acid sensing of minimal residual acetic acid on the quadrant mediated by the Ir8a/Ir64a complex (Ai et al., 2010) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ai et al., 2010 showing Ir8a/Ir64a mediates acid sensing, and by data showing that orco, Ir8a double mutants no longer show repulsion (Figure 2C), and that neutralized apple cider vinegar eliminates the repulsion (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: The orco, Ir8a double mutant was no longer repelled by the odor quadrant.
source: Indeed, the orco, Ir8a double mutant was no longer repelled by the odor quadrant (Figure 2C), and the use of neutralized apple cider vinegar as the stimulus eliminated the post-stimulus repulsion demonstrated by orco mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Behavioral data show orco/Ir8a double mutants had reduced repulsion compared to orco mutants alone (Figure 2C).

claim: Neutralized apple cider vinegar eliminates the post-stimulus repulsion demonstrated by orco mutants.
source: Indeed, the orco, Ir8a double mutant was no longer repelled by the odor quadrant (Figure 2C), and the use of neutralized apple cider vinegar as the stimulus eliminated the post-stimulus repulsion demonstrated by orco mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Behavioral data show orco mutants tested with neutralized apple cider vinegar (pH=7.0) no longer showed post-stimulus repulsion (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: Acidity of apple cider vinegar is not necessary for triggering wild-type post-stimulation behavior.
source: We further tested if acidity of the apple cider vinegar was necessary for triggering wild-type post-stimulation behavior by neutralizing apple cider vinegar to pH = 7.0. No phenotypic difference was found compared to non-neutralized apple cider vinegar (pH = 3.2) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Behavioral data show wild-type flies exhibited similar post-stimulus aggregation with neutralized (pH=7.0) and non-neutralized (pH=3.2) apple cider vinegar (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).

claim: Detection of the food-odor-induced pheromone is mediated through the orco-dependent olfactory system.
source: In sum, these data suggest that detection of the food-odor-induced pheromone is mediated through the orco-dependent olfactory system.
evidence: This conclusion is based on data showing that orco mutants completely lack pheromone attraction, while gustatory (Poxn), ppk23, and ionotropic receptor (Ir8a/Ir25a) mutants show normal aggregation.

claim: cVA is not the food-odor induced aggregation pheromone.
source: Mutations of the key components in the signaling pathway (Or67d, lush, snmp) do not alter the post-stimulus aggregation behavior (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), suggesting that cVA is not the food-odor induced aggregation pheromone.
evidence: Behavioral data show that mutants of Or67d, lush, and snmp exhibited similar post-stimulus aggregation to wild-type (Figure 2—figure supplement 4, p = 0.4405).

claim: Hexane can extract the active pheromone off the glass surface in the food-odor-induced quadrant.
source: Since most insect pheromones are lipophilic carbohydrates dissolvable in hexane (van der Goes van Naters and Carlson, 2007), we reasoned that hexane might extract the active pheromone off the glass surface in the food-odor-induced quadrant.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral experiments showing that naïve flies could trace and follow an 'E' pattern painted with hexane extracts from pheromone-deposited glass plates (Figure 3A, B, Video 3).

claim: Naïve flies can trace and follow patterns painted with hexane extracts of pheromone deposits.
source: We induced wild-type flies to deposit the food-odor induced pheromone onto the glass plate and dissolved the deposited molecules into hexane. We then painted the hexane extract onto a new glass plate in a letter 'E' pattern. Naïve new flies were able to trace and follow the E pattern but do not follow control hexane extracts of flies stimulated by humidified air painted in the same pattern (Figure 3A, B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Video 3).
evidence: Behavioral tracking data show flies following the 'E' pattern painted with pheromone extract but not control extract (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Video 3).

claim: The pheromone is volatile.
source: Behavioral results suggested the pheromone was volatile because: 1) it required the olfactory system for detection (Figure 2C); 2) constant air flushing reduced behavioral attraction after ∼25 min (Figure 1—figure supplement 5); and 3) heating the pheromone-containing arena to 32°C to increase odor volatility eliminated post-stimulus behaviors (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Multiple lines of evidence support volatility: requirement for olfactory system, reduction over time with air flushing, and elimination of behavior with heating.

claim: cVA was not detected in pheromone extracts from the glass plates.
source: Consistent with behavioral results that cVA is unlikely to be the food-odor induced pheromone (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), cVA was not detected in pheromone extracts from the glass plates (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: GC-MS analysis of hexane extracts did not detect cVA (Supplementary file 1).

claim: 7-docosene and 23-methyldocosane were not detected in pheromone extracts.
source: 7-docosene and 23-methyldocosane were also not detected, while 5-tricosene was detected at trace amounts (Figure 3C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: GC-MS analysis results (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 1).

claim: 5-tricosene was detected at trace amounts in pheromone extracts.
source: 7-docosene and 23-methyldocosane were also not detected, while 5-tricosene was detected at trace amounts (Figure 3C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: GC-MS analysis results (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 1).

claim: Levels of 7-tricosene were increased in the experimental conditions but behavioral results excluded it as the food-odor-induced pheromone.
source: The levels of 7-tricosene were increased in the experimental conditions. However, our behavioral results excluded 7-tricosene as the food-odor-induced pheromone (Figure 2B; also see below and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: GC-MS showed increased 7-tricosene, but ppk23 mutants (which cannot detect 7-tricosene) showed normal aggregation (Figure 2B), and 7-tricosene induced neutral to slightly repulsive behavior (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).

claim: 9-tricosene was significantly enriched in the experimental but not humidified air + flies control group.
source: Interestingly, only one other peak was significantly enriched in the experimental but not humidified air + flies control group: (Z) 9-tricosene (9-T) (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: GC-MS analysis showed 9-tricosene exhibited a 2.8 fold enrichment on glass plates upon food-odor stimulation (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 1).

claim: 9-tricosene is a male-specific volatile pheromone in D. melanogaster.
source: Little is known regarding the function of 9-tricosene in D. melanogaster besides its presence as a male-specific volatile pheromone (Everaerts et al., 2010; Farine et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies identifying 9-tricosene as male-specific and volatile (Everaerts et al., 2010; Farine et al., 2012).

claim: 9-tricosene elicits attraction behaviors in Drosophila.
source: To determine if 9-tricosene was attractive to Drosophila, as would be predicted for the food-odor induced aggregation pheromone, we used 9-tricosene as the stimulus in the 4-field olfactory assay. Indeed, 9-tricosene elicits attraction behaviors (Figure 3D-E, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Behavioral data show dose-dependent attraction to 9-tricosene (Figure 3D-E).

claim: Naïve flies trace and follow 9-tricosene patterns, paying particular attention to the odor border.
source: To determine if 9-tricosene could direct aggregation behaviors, we repeated the 'E' experiment using 9-tricosene alone (Figure 3F). Naïve flies did trace and follow the 9-tricosene pattern, paying particular attention to the odor border (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Behavioral tracking data show flies following 9-tricosene 'E' pattern with preference for borders (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).

claim: Flies appear to be repelled by the center of a concentrated 9-tricosene odor trail.
source: Nonetheless, the aggregation response was not identical to the full hexane extract. In particular, flies appeared to be repelled by the center of a concentrated 9-tricosene odor trail.
evidence: Behavioral observations from the 'E' pattern experiment (Figure 3F) show flies avoiding the center of concentrated 9-tricosene deposits.

claim: 9-tricosene under certain conditions can function as an aggregation pheromone, although additional pheromone components may contribute to the full aggregation phenotype.
source: Overall, these data suggest that 9-tricosene under certain conditions can function as an aggregation pheromone, although additional pheromone components may contribute to the full aggregation phenotype.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that 9-tricosene alone shows some but not all characteristics of the full pheromone extract in behavioral assays.

claim: 9-tricosene and other cuticular hydrocarbons are produced by oenocytes on the fly abdominal wall.
source: 9-Tricosene is a member of cuticular hydrocarbons produced by oenocytes on the fly abdominal wall (Billeter et al., 2009; Everaerts et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing oenocytes produce cuticular hydrocarbons including 9-tricosene (Billeter et al., 2009; Everaerts et al., 2010).

claim: Oenocyte-less males mixed with wild-type females no longer produced post-stimulus aggregation behavior.
source: Oenocyte-less males mixed with wild-type females no longer produced a post-stimulus aggregation behavior, suggesting that an oenocyte-derived cuticular hydrocarbon is essential for post-stimulus aggregation (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Behavioral data show reduced post-stimulus aggregation when oenocyte-ablated males were used as depositors (Figure 3—figure supplement 4, p = 0.0021).

claim: An oenocyte-derived cuticular hydrocarbon is essential for post-stimulus aggregation.
source: Oenocyte-less males mixed with wild-type females no longer produced a post-stimulus aggregation behavior, suggesting that an oenocyte-derived cuticular hydrocarbon is essential for post-stimulus aggregation (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This inference is based on the observation that ablating oenocytes, which produce cuticular hydrocarbons including 9-tricosene, eliminates post-stimulus aggregation.

claim: The orco mutants completely lacked responses to 9-tricosene in electroantennogram recordings.
source: The orco mutants completely lacked responses to 9-tricosene (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—source data 1). This suggests that 9-tricosene activates an orco-dependent odorant receptor, and does not require signaling from Ir or Gr receptors.
evidence: EAG recordings show no response to 9-tricosene in orco mutants compared to wild-type (Figure 4A,B).

claim: 9-tricosene activates an orco-dependent odorant receptor and does not require signaling from Ir or Gr receptors.
source: The orco mutants completely lacked responses to 9-tricosene (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—source data 1). This suggests that 9-tricosene activates an orco-dependent odorant receptor, and does not require signaling from Ir or Gr receptors.
evidence: This inference is based on EAG data showing complete loss of 9-tricosene response in orco mutants.

claim: 9-tricosene elicits rapid and robust firing patterns in the antennal basiconic ab4 sensillum.
source: We found that 9-tricosene elicits rapid and robust firing patterns in the antennal basiconic ab4 sensillum, which houses two neurons (ab4A and ab4B) that express Or7a (ab4A) or Or56a receptors (ab4B) (Figure 4C) (Couto et al., 2005; Fishilevich and Vosshall, 2005; Stensmyr et al., 2012).
evidence: Single sensillum recording data show robust responses to 9-tricosene in ab4 sensilla (Figure 4C).

claim: 9-tricosene stimulates spiking of the larger amplitude neuron in ab4 sensillum, indicating the 9-tricosene-responsive ORNs are ab4A, which express Or7a receptors.
source: 9-Tricosene stimulates spiking of the larger amplitude neuron indicating the 9-tricosene-responsive ORNs are ab4A, which express Or7a receptors.
evidence: Single sensillum recording traces show activation of the larger amplitude spike in ab4 sensilla upon 9-tricosene stimulation (Figure 4D).

claim: Stimulation of ab4 sensilla by flies pre-stimulated with apple cider vinegar led to significant increases in ab4A (Or7a) activation compared to flies pre-stimulated with dry air.
source: Stimulation of ab4 sensilla by flies housed in a glass vial pre-stimulated with apple cider vinegar, compared to flies pre-stimulated with dry air alone, also led to significant increases in ab4A (Or7a) activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Single sensillum recording data show increased ab4 spike frequency when stimulated with flies pre-exposed to apple cider vinegar versus dry air (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, p = 0.03).

claim: Or7a is a broadly tuned receptor that responds to a broad range of odors, including many aldehydes and alcohols.
source: The identification of Or7a as a 9-tricosene pheromone receptor was surprising as, unlike previously identified pheromone receptors, it had been shown to respond to a broad range of odors, including many aldehydes and alcohols (Hallem et al., 2004; Hallem and Carlson, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comprehensive studies characterizing Or7a responses to multiple odorants (Hallem et al., 2004; Hallem and Carlson, 2006).

claim: Expression of Or7a in ab3A neurons endows them the ability to respond to 9-tricosene comparable to endogenous Or7a-positive ab4 sensillum.
source: To determine if the Or7a receptor is sufficient for 9-tricosene responses, we misexpressed Or7a in an olfactory neuron that lacks an odorant receptor in ab3A sensillar neurons (Dobritsa et al., 2003). Expression of Or7a endowed ab3A neurons the ability to respond to 9-tricosene comparable to the 9-tricosene activation pattern detected in endogenous Or7a-positive ab4 sensillum (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: Single sensillum recording data show that ab3 neurons expressing Or7a respond to 9-tricosene similarly to native ab4 neurons (Figure 4D,E).

claim: The Or7a receptor responds to 9-tricosene.
source: These data indicate that the Or7a receptor responds to 9-tricosene.
evidence: This conclusion is based on data showing Or7a is necessary (Or7a mutants lack response) and sufficient (misexpression confers response) for 9-tricosene detection.

claim: Basiconic sensilla were traditionally considered food odor detectors.
source: This is unexpected since basiconic sensilla were traditionally considered food odor detectors (Larsson et al., 2004; Suh et al., 2004; Fishilevich and Vosshall, 2005; Jones et al., 2007; Laissue and Vosshall, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies characterizing basiconic sensilla as responding to food odors.

claim: Both male and female ab4A/Or7a neurons responded equally to 9-tricosene.
source: Both male and female ab4A/Or7a neurons responded equally to 9-tricosene (Figure 4E), consistent with 9-tricosene being attractive to both males and females (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: Single sensillum recording data show similar responses to 9-tricosene in male and female ab4 neurons (Figure 4E).

claim: Or7a neurons did not respond to cVA.
source: Or7a neurons did not respond to cVA (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Single sensillum recording data show no significant response of ab4 sensilla to various concentrations of cVA (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).

claim: No spontaneous or 9-tricosene stimulated ab4A spiking activity was observed in Or7a mutant flies.
source: Ab4 sensilla in Or7a mutants were identified based on their shape and the specific response of the ab4B neuron to geosmin (Stensmyr et al., 2012). No spontaneous or 9-tricosene stimulated ab4A spiking activity was observed in Or7a mutant flies (Figure 4F,G), indicating that Or7a is necessary for 9-tricosene activation in ab4 sensilla.
evidence: Single sensillum recording data show complete loss of ab4A response to 9-tricosene in Or7a mutants while ab4B response to geosmin remains intact (Figure 4F,G).

claim: Or7a is necessary for 9-tricosene activation in ab4 sensilla.
source: No spontaneous or 9-tricosene stimulated ab4A spiking activity was observed in Or7a mutant flies (Figure 4F,G), indicating that Or7a is necessary for 9-tricosene activation in ab4 sensilla.
evidence: Single sensillum recording data from Or7a mutants show no ab4A response to 9-tricosene (Figure 4F,G).

claim: 9-tricosene specifically activates the 'generalist' Or7a receptor.
source: All together, these data suggest that 9-tricosene specifically activates the 'generalist' Or7a receptor.
evidence: This conclusion is based on electrophysiological data showing Or7a is necessary and sufficient for 9-tricosene responses, combined with previous knowledge that Or7a responds to many odorants.

claim: Or7a-GAL4 specifically drives effector expression only in olfactory neurons that target the DL5 antennal lobe glomerulus.
source: Or7a-GAL4 specifically drives effector expression only in olfactory neurons that target the DL5 antennal lobe glomerulus (Figure 5A) (Couto et al., 2005).
evidence: Immunostaining data show Or7a-expressing neurons innervating the DL5 glomerulus (Figure 5A), consistent with previous characterization (Couto et al., 2005).

claim: Or7a expression was not detected outside the antennae.
source: We did not detect expression outside the antennae (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Imaging of Or7a-GAL4 expression in whole animals, dissected brain and ventral nerve cord showed expression only in antennal olfactory neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Aggregation responses to naturally deposited food-odor induced pheromone were completely abolished in Or7a neuron-ablated flies.
source: Aggregation responses to both the naturally deposited food-odor induced pheromone (Figure 5B,C, Figure 5—source data 1) and to 9-tricosene (Figure 5D,E) were completely abolished in Or7a neuron-ablated flies obtained using Or7a-Gal4+UAS-hid (Figure 5) or Or7a-Gal4+UAS-DTI (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Behavioral data show Or7a neuron-ablated flies (Or7a-Gal4/UAS-hid) had significantly reduced post-stimulus aggregation to natural pheromone (Figure 5B,C, p = 0.0012) and to 9-tricosene (Figure 5D,E, p < 0.001).

claim: Aggregation responses to 9-tricosene were completely abolished in Or7a neuron-ablated flies.
source: Aggregation responses to both the naturally deposited food-odor induced pheromone (Figure 5B,C, Figure 5—source data 1) and to 9-tricosene (Figure 5D,E) were completely abolished in Or7a neuron-ablated flies obtained using Or7a-Gal4+UAS-hid (Figure 5) or Or7a-Gal4+UAS-DTI (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Behavioral data show Or7a neuron-ablated flies had no attraction to 9-tricosene (Figure 5D,E; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: Ablation of other odorant receptors (OrX-Gal4+UAS-hid) did not affect aggregation.
source: Ablation of other odorant receptors (OrX-Gal4+UAS-hid) did not affect aggregation (Figure 5C).
evidence: Behavioral data show that ablation of Or83c, Or43a, and Or88a neurons did not significantly affect post-stimulus aggregation (Figure 5C).

claim: Or7a mutants completely lacked attraction to the naturally deposited food-odor-induced pheromone.
source: Similarly, Or7a mutants completely lacked attraction to the naturally deposited food-odor-induced pheromone and to 9-tricosene (Figure 5B-E).
evidence: Behavioral data show Or7a mutants had significantly reduced post-stimulus aggregation to natural pheromone (Figure 5B,C, p = 0.006) and to 9-tricosene (Figure 5D,E).

claim: Or7a mutants completely lacked attraction to 9-tricosene.
source: Similarly, Or7a mutants completely lacked attraction to the naturally deposited food-odor-induced pheromone and to 9-tricosene (Figure 5B-E).
evidence: Behavioral data show Or7a mutants had no significant attraction to 9-tricosene (Figure 5D,E).

claim: 7-tricosene induced a neutral to slightly repulsive behavior in wild-type flies.
source: To verify that aggregation behavior is specific to 9-tricosene, we repeated the experiments using the 9-tricosene pheromone isomer 7-tricosene (7-T), which contains an identical carbon chain length to 9-tricosene but a double bond at an alternate location. Interestingly, 7-tricosene induced a neutral to slightly repulsive behavior in WT flies (AI = −0.07 ± 0.026, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Behavioral data show wild-type flies exhibited slight repulsion to 7-tricosene (Figure 5—figure supplement 3, AI = -0.07).

claim: Aggregation behavior to the naturally deposited food-odor-induced pheromone depends on 9-tricosene and proper function of the Or7a receptor.
source: These data suggest that aggregation behavior to the naturally deposited food-odor-induced pheromone depends on 9-tricosene and proper function of the Or7a receptor.
evidence: This conclusion is based on data showing that Or7a mutants and Or7a neuron-ablated flies lack aggregation to both natural pheromone and 9-tricosene, while 7-tricosene (which differs only in double bond position) does not induce aggregation.

claim: A deposited pheromone could guide female egg-laying site selection decisions.
source: Under conditions in which the food-odor-stimulated pheromone was deposited onto the agarose (Figure 6A′), females laid five-fold more eggs in the pheromone quadrant. This suggests that a deposited pheromone could guide female egg-laying site selection decisions.
evidence: Behavioral data show significantly more eggs laid in the pheromone quadrant compared to control quadrants (Figure 6A′, p < 0.001).

claim: Female flies laid significantly more eggs in locations containing only 9-tricosene.
source: We next generated an arena in which one quadrant contained 9-tricosene (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). Female flies also laid significantly more eggs in locations containing only 9-tricosene (Figure 6B′).
evidence: Behavioral data show significantly more eggs laid in the 9-tricosene quadrant (Figure 6B′, p < 0.001).

claim: The 9-tricosene egg-laying preference was abolished when Or7a neurons were ablated.
source: The 9-tricosene egg-laying preference was abolished when Or7a neurons were ablated (Or7a-Gal4/UAS-hid or Or7a-Gal4/UAS-DTI) (Figure 6C′ and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Behavioral data show Or7a neuron-ablated flies showed no significant egg-laying preference for 9-tricosene quadrant (Figure 6C′, p = 0.384; Figure 6—figure supplement 2, p = 0.1349).

claim: The 9-tricosene guided egg laying preference was abolished in Or7a mutant flies.
source: The 9-tricosene guided egg laying preference was also abolished in Or7a mutant flies (Figure 6D).
evidence: Behavioral data show Or7a mutants showed no significant egg-laying preference for 9-tricosene (Figure 6D, p = 0.69).

claim: The oviposition preference for the 9-tricosene quadrant was not due to innate attraction to 9-tricosene because females spent similar time in the four quadrants over the 23 hr egg-laying assay.
source: The oviposition preference for the 9-tricosene quadrant was not due to the innate attraction to 9-tricosene because females spent similar time in the four quadrants over the course of the 23 hr egg-laying assay (Figure 6E).
evidence: Positional tracking data over 23 hours show no significant positional preference for the 9-tricosene quadrant (Figure 6E, p = 0.1).

claim: Female flies did not preferentially oviposit in the 7-tricosene quadrant.
source: To verify that oviposition guidance is specific to 9-tricosene, we repeated the oviposition experiments using the 9-tricosene pheromone isomer 7-tricosene (7-T), the most abundant cuticular hydrocarbon in male flies (Everaerts et al., 2010). Female flies did not preferentially oviposit in the 7-T quadrant (Figure 6F).
evidence: Behavioral data show no significant egg-laying preference for 7-tricosene quadrant (Figure 6F, p = 0.28).

claim: Total egg numbers laid were significantly higher in Or7a mutant and Or7a neuron ablated flies.
source: Interestingly, total egg numbers laid were significant higher in Or7a mutant and Or7a neuron ablated flies, implying a potential connection of oviposition site selection and egg deposition number (Figure 6G).
evidence: Behavioral data show increased total egg numbers in Or7a mutants and Or7a neuron-ablated flies compared to wild-type (Figure 6G, p = 0.0021 and 0.0001).

claim: Or7a is expressed only in the antennae and not in the female ovipositor.
source: However, since Or7a is expressed only in the antennae and not in the female ovipositor (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), this implicates Or7a signaling in the antennae as the main driver of Or7a-directed oviposition guidance.
evidence: Expression analysis shows Or7a-GAL4 expression only in antennae, not in ovipositor or other tissues (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Or7a signaling in the antennae is the main driver of Or7a-directed oviposition guidance.
source: However, since Or7a is expressed only in the antennae and not in the female ovipositor (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), this implicates Or7a signaling in the antennae as the main driver of Or7a-directed oviposition guidance.
evidence: This inference is based on the observation that Or7a is only expressed in antennae, yet Or7a function is necessary for oviposition guidance.

claim: Male derived 9-tricosene can guide female egg-laying preferences, and this decision-making process requires proper antennal Or7a neuronal function.
source: All together, these data suggest that male derived 9-tricosene can guide female egg-laying preferences, and this decision-making process requires proper antennal Or7a neuronal function.
evidence: This conclusion is based on data showing that 9-tricosene guides oviposition in wild-type but not Or7a mutant or Or7a neuron-ablated flies, and that Or7a is expressed only in antennae.

claim: E2-hexenal was identified as the most potent ligand for Or7a.
source: Comprehensive SSR surveys of odorant–receptor activities identified multiple ligands for the Or7a receptor (Hallem and Carlson, 2006). E2-hexenal, a leafy green volatile released upon fruit or leaf damage (Myung et al., 2006), was identified as the most potent ligand for Or7a (Hallem and Carlson, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comprehensive characterization studies (Hallem and Carlson, 2006; Myung et al., 2006).

claim: E2-hexenal is a leafy green volatile released upon fruit or leaf damage.
source: E2-hexenal, a leafy green volatile released upon fruit or leaf damage (Myung et al., 2006), was identified as the most potent ligand for Or7a (Hallem and Carlson, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study characterizing E2-hexenal release (Myung et al., 2006).

claim: E2-hexenal directed Or7a-dependent egg-laying site selection.
source: We thus examined if E2-hexenal could direct similar behaviors as those triggered by 9-tricosene (Figure 7, Figure 7—source data 1). Indeed, we found that E2-hexenal, like 9-tricosene, directed Or7a-dependent egg-laying site selection (Figure 7A-D) and attraction (Figure 7E).
evidence: Behavioral data show E2-hexenal guided egg-laying site selection in wild-type but not Or7a mutant flies (Figure 7C,D).

claim: E2-hexenal directed Or7a-dependent attraction.
source: Indeed, we found that E2-hexenal, like 9-tricosene, directed Or7a-dependent egg-laying site selection (Figure 7A-D) and attraction (Figure 7E).
evidence: Behavioral data show E2-hexenal elicited attraction in wild-type flies that was significantly reduced in Or7a mutants (Figure 7E, p = 0.0149).

claim: 9-tricosene can effectively guide oviposition in the surrounding presence of low and middle, but not high, E2-hexenal concentrations.
source: To determine if 9-tricosene pheromone cues remained recognizable in a surrounding of E2-hexenal, we repeated the 9-tricosene (10−4 concentration) 3-choice oviposition-selection assays in the presence of high (10−6, 10−7), middle (10−8) or low (10−9,10−10) E2-hexenal concentrations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). 9-tricosene functioned as an oviposition guidance cue in the presence of low and middle, but not high, E2-hexenal concentrations.
evidence: Behavioral data show 9-tricosene guided oviposition in presence of low and middle E2-hexenal concentrations, but high E2-hexenal concentrations were more potent than 9-tricosene (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: All odorants that activated Or7a directed positive oviposition-site selection to some degree.
source: We therefore tested the oviposition-site selection guidance to 3 additional Or7a-agonists (benzaldeyde, 1-butanol, 1-propanol) as well as 3 odorants that do not activate Or7a (hexyl butyrate, pentanoic acid, ethyl lactate) (Hallem and Carlson, 2006). Interestingly, all odorants that activated Or7a directed positive oviposition-site selection to some degree, whereas all odorants not activating Or7a showed mainly neutral or negative oviposition-site selection effects (Figure 8).
evidence: Behavioral data show that Or7a agonists (benzaldehyde, 1-butanol, 1-propanol) all showed positive oviposition preference indices, while non-Or7a agonists showed neutral or negative preferences (Figure 8, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).

claim: All odorants not activating Or7a showed mainly neutral or negative oviposition-site selection effects.
source: Interestingly, all odorants that activated Or7a directed positive oviposition-site selection to some degree, whereas all odorants not activating Or7a showed mainly neutral or negative oviposition-site selection effects (Figure 8).
evidence: Behavioral data show that non-Or7a agonists (hexyl butyrate, pentanoic acid, ethyl lactate) showed neutral or negative oviposition preference indices (Figure 8, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).

claim: Egg-laying site selection was associated with the specificity of the odorant for Or7a: more specific Or7a agonists demonstrated higher positive oviposition site selection.
source: Egg-laying site selection was associated with the specificity of the odorant for Or7a: those odorants (e.g., benzaldehyde or 1-butanol) that activated many additional odorant receptors exhibited decreased oviposition towards that odorant whereas more specific Or7a agonists (e.g., 9-tricosene and 1-propanol) demonstrated the highest positive oviposition site selection (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Behavioral data show correlation between Or7a specificity and oviposition preference, with 9-tricosene and 1-propanol (more specific) showing higher preference than benzaldehyde and 1-butanol (less specific) (Figure 8, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).

claim: Selective optogenetic stimulation of Or7a neurons was sufficient to guide egg-laying site selection.
source: Indeed, selective optogenetic stimulation of Or7a neurons was also sufficient to guide egg-laying site selection.
evidence: Optogenetic experiments show that flies fed all-trans-retinal (enabling CsChrimson activation) exhibited significantly increased egg-laying preference for the red light quadrant compared to flies not fed all-trans-retinal (Figure 8—figure supplement 2, p = 0.022).

claim: Or7a neuron activation can influence egg-laying decisions.
source: These results support the findings that Or7a neuron activity can influence egg-laying decisions.
evidence: This conclusion is based on optogenetic data showing that specific activation of Or7a neurons guides oviposition site selection (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).

claim: Aggregation at a food-site might be strongly influenced by the olfactory perception of an optimal food source.
source: Our results suggest that aggregation at a food-site might be strongly influenced by the olfactory perception of an optimal food source.
evidence: This inference is based on observations that aggregation pheromone is only deposited upon food-odor stimulations (apple cider vinegar, banana, yeast) but not by attractive single components (ethyl acetate).

claim: An aggregation pheromone is only deposited upon food-odor stimulations such as apple cider vinegar, ripe banana and yeast.
source: We found that an aggregation pheromone is only deposited upon food-odor stimulations, such as apple cider vinegar, ripe banana and yeast.
evidence: Behavioral data show post-stimulus aggregation occurs after apple cider vinegar, banana, and yeast stimulation but not after ethyl acetate or humidified air (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).

claim: An attractive odorant component (ethyl acetate) found in apple cider vinegar was not sufficient for pheromone deposition.
source: An attractive odorant component (ethyl acetate) found in apple cider vinegar was not sufficient for pheromone deposition, suggesting that attraction per se to an odor is not sufficient for aggregation pheromone deposition.
evidence: Behavioral data show ethyl acetate was attractive but did not induce post-stimulus aggregation (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).

claim: Attraction per se to an odor is not sufficient for aggregation pheromone deposition.
source: An attractive odorant component (ethyl acetate) found in apple cider vinegar was not sufficient for pheromone deposition, suggesting that attraction per se to an odor is not sufficient for aggregation pheromone deposition.
evidence: This inference is based on the observation that ethyl acetate is attractive but does not induce pheromone deposition.

claim: cVA is only weakly attractive on its own.
source: However, in contrast to aggregation pheromones identified in other Drosophila species (Bartelt et al., 1985; Hedlund et al., 1996), cVA is only weakly attractive on its own (Xu et al., 2005), although does enhance aggregation when coupled with food or food-derived odors (Bartelt et al., 1985; Everaerts et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies characterizing cVA attraction properties (Bartelt et al., 1985; Hedlund et al., 1996; Xu et al., 2005; Everaerts et al., 2010).

claim: cVA enhances aggregation when coupled with food or food-derived odors.
source: However, in contrast to aggregation pheromones identified in other Drosophila species (Bartelt et al., 1985; Hedlund et al., 1996), cVA is only weakly attractive on its own (Xu et al., 2005), although does enhance aggregation when coupled with food or food-derived odors (Bartelt et al., 1985; Everaerts et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing cVA's role in aggregation with food odors (Bartelt et al., 1985; Everaerts et al., 2010).

claim: Mutating key components in the cVA signaling pathway did not affect the food-odor induced aggregation behavior.
source: However, mutating key components in the cVA signaling pathway did not affect the food-odor induced aggregation behavior.
evidence: Behavioral data show Or67d, lush, and snmp mutants exhibited normal post-stimulus aggregation (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).

claim: GC-MS analysis of the active aggregation pheromone extract found no evidence that cVA was deposited.
source: Moreover, GC–MS analysis of the active aggregation pheromone extract found no evidence that cVA was deposited.
evidence: GC-MS data show cVA was not detected in pheromone extracts (Supplementary file 1).

claim: cVA is likely not responsible for the aggregation behaviors triggered by food odors in these experiments.
source: Therefore, cVA is likely not responsible for the aggregation behaviors triggered by food odors in these experiments.
evidence: This conclusion is based on genetic data showing cVA pathway mutants have normal aggregation, and chemical data showing cVA is not detected in pheromone extracts.

claim: Under natural conditions, cVA may be used as a long distance co-attractant with food odors at mating sites while 9-tricosene is used as a short-range aggregation pheromone at food sites.
source: Nonetheless, it remains possible that under natural conditions, cVA is used as a long distance co-attractant with food odors at mating sites while 9-tricosene is used as a short-range aggregation pheromone at food sites.
evidence: This is speculation based on the different properties of cVA (volatile, works with food odors) and 9-tricosene (low volatility, food-odor induced).

claim: Pheromone trails play an important role in organizing social foraging behaviors for many flying and non-flying insects.
source: For many flying and non-flying insects, pheromone trails play an important role in organizing social foraging behaviors (Schorkopf et al., 2007; Wyatt, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to reviews on insect pheromone communication (Schorkopf et al., 2007; Wyatt, 2014).

claim: The first animals to find a suitable food source use a pheromone trail to recruit more animals to the food source, establishing a positive feedback of pheromone signaling.
source: The first animals to find a suitable food source use a pheromone trail to recruit even more animals to the food source, which in turn deposit additional pheromone trails, and thereby establish a positive feedback of pheromone signaling towards the foraging site (Schorkopf et al., 2007; Wyatt, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations describing pheromone trail recruitment mechanisms (Schorkopf et al., 2007; Wyatt, 2014).

claim: The experiments identified pheromone tags deposited when D. melanogaster males perceived food odors, implicating the existence of pheromone trail behavior in this insect.
source: Our experiments identified pheromone tags deposited when D. melanogaster males perceived food odors, implicating the existence of such a behavioral occurrence in this insect.
evidence: This inference is based on experimental data showing food-odor-induced pheromone deposition by males that guides aggregation.

claim: 9-tricosene and Or7a neuron activities are likely key mediators of pheromone trail response.
source: We found that 9-tricosene, and Or7a neuron activities, are likely key mediators of this particular pheromone response.
evidence: This conclusion is based on data showing 9-tricosene is the deposited pheromone and Or7a is necessary and sufficient for its detection and behavioral responses.

claim: The 'E' experiments with 9-tricosene suggest that 9-tricosene may cause repulsion at high concentrations.
source: Interestingly, the 'E' experiments with 9-tricosene suggests that 9-tricosene may cause repulsion at high concentrations, although it remains to be determined if these high concentrations represent natural conditions.
evidence: Behavioral observations from the 'E' pattern experiment show flies avoiding the center of concentrated 9-tricosene deposits (Figure 3F).

claim: E2-hexenal, because of its high volatility, might represent a long-distance cue for recently fallen fruit or plants.
source: E2-hexenal, because of its high volatility, might represent such a long-distance cue for recently fallen fruit or plants.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known high volatility of E2-hexenal and its release from damaged plant material.

claim: E2-hexenal levels will diminish over extended time periods because it is generated by a plant-dependent enzymatic reaction.
source: Since E2-hexenal is generated by a plant-dependent enzymatic reaction, its levels will diminish over extended time periods (Farag and Pare, 2002q; Myung et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies characterizing E2-hexenal production mechanisms (Farag and Pare, 2002q; Myung et al., 2006).

claim: 9-tricosene, as a low volatility olfactory pheromone, might be ideally suited as a stable close-range olfactory marker to convey environmental conditions.
source: In contrast, 9-tricosene, as a low volatility olfactory pheromone, might be ideally suited as a stable close-range olfactory marker and utilized to convey environmental conditions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the chemical properties of 9-tricosene (low volatility, stability) and its behavioral functions.

claim: 9-tricosene is a sex attractant for female houseflies (Musca domestica).
source: For instance, 9-tricosene is a sex attractant for female houseflies (Musca domestica) (Carlson et al., 1971) and honey bee waggle dancers (Apis mellifera) use a pheromone cocktail that includes 9-tricosene to communicate with nest mates about the locations of food sources (Thom et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study identifying 9-tricosene function in houseflies (Carlson et al., 1971).

claim: Honey bee waggle dancers (Apis mellifera) use a pheromone cocktail that includes 9-tricosene to communicate with nest mates about the locations of food sources.
source: For instance, 9-tricosene is a sex attractant for female houseflies (Musca domestica) (Carlson et al., 1971) and honey bee waggle dancers (Apis mellifera) use a pheromone cocktail that includes 9-tricosene to communicate with nest mates about the locations of food sources (Thom et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on honey bee communication (Thom et al., 2007).

claim: 9-tricosene represents the first Drosophila cuticular hydrocarbon pheromone demonstrated to activate a Drosophila basiconic sensilla.
source: 9-tricosene represents the first Drosophila cuticular hydrocarbon pheromone that, to our knowledge, is demonstrated to activate a Drosophila basiconic sensilla.
evidence: This claim is based on the novel finding that 9-tricosene activates ab4 basiconic sensilla, contrasting with previous knowledge that pheromones typically activate trichoid sensilla.

claim: The same ab4 sensilla and Or7a olfactory receptor responds to the silk moth pheromone bombykol.
source: Intriguingly, the same sensilla and Or7a olfactory receptor responds to the silk moth pheromone bombykol (Syed et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study showing Or7a responds to bombykol (Syed et al., 2006).

claim: The Drosophila Or7a neuron's response to bombykol might represent off-target ligand specificity for 9-tricosene.
source: It is interesting to speculate that this Drosophila neuron's response to bombykol might represent off-target ligand specificity for 9-tricosene.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that Or7a responds to both 9-tricosene and bombykol.

claim: Activation of odorant receptors by both pheromone and plant volatiles might be more widespread than previously anticipated.
source: Our data further suggests that activation of odorant receptors by both pheromone and plant volatiles might be more widespread than previously anticipated.
evidence: This inference is based on the finding that Or7a responds to both the pheromone 9-tricosene and the plant volatile E2-hexenal, and is supported by a citation showing a moth pheromone receptor also responds to a plant volatile (Rouyar et al., 2015).

claim: An olfactory receptor in the moth Agrotis ipsilon that was previously considered pheromone specific was recently found to also respond to the plant volatile heptanal.
source: Indeed, an olfactory receptor in the moth Agrotis ipsilon that was previously considered to be pheromone specific was recently found to also respond to the plant volatile heptanal, despite the plant volatile showing no structural similarity to the moth pheromone (Rouyar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study on moth olfactory receptors (Rouyar et al., 2015).

claim: Oviposition site selection comprises three steps: an ovipositor motor program, a clean/rest period and a search-like behavior.
source: The behavior comprises three steps—an ovipositor motor program, a clean/rest period and a search-like behavior.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study characterizing oviposition behavior (Yang et al., 2008).

claim: The ovipositor motor program that leads to egg deposition is relatively short (6-7 s) compared to clean/rest and search-like behaviors (100-130 s).
source: The ovipositor motor program that leads to egg deposition is relatively short (6–7 s) as compared to clean/rest and search-like behaviors (100–130 s) (Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study quantifying oviposition behavior timing (Yang et al., 2008).

claim: 9-tricosene might mediate two temporally distinct responses: a short-term aggregation behavior lasting ~25 min and a long-term oviposition site selection behavior lasting for hours.
source: These findings also suggest that 9-tricosene might mediate two temporally distinct responses in our experimental design. A short-term aggregation behavior that lasts ∼25 min and a long-term oviposition site selection behavior that lasts for hours.
evidence: This speculation is based on observations that aggregation lasts ~25 min while oviposition preference persists for 23 hours without positional preference.

claim: A possible mechanism underlying different temporal behaviors could be that detection thresholds for the two behaviors are different, with higher 9-tricosene concentrations triggering aggregation and low concentrations affecting oviposition.
source: A possible mechanism underlying these different behaviors could be that detection thresholds for the two behaviors are different, that is, higher concentrations of 9-tricosene triggers aggregation whereas low 9-tricosene concentrations affect oviposition.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms for the observed temporal differences in behavior.

claim: In many insects, eggs are vulnerable and larvae have restricted motility, thus oviposition site selection is a crucial decision for progeny survival.
source: In many insects, eggs are vulnerable and larvae have restricted motility, thus oviposition site selection is a crucial decision for progeny survival.
evidence: This is general knowledge about insect biology and the importance of oviposition decisions.

claim: The hypothesis of 'mother-knows-best' stipulates that female egg-laying decisions evolved to oviposit in places offering the best survival of offspring.
source: The hypothesis of 'mother-knows-best' stipulates that female egg-laying decisions evolved to oviposit in places offering the best survival of offspring (Soto et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on oviposition decision-making (Soto et al., 2014).

claim: Oviposition decisions require multiple sensory modalities, such as visual, olfactory, gustatory and proprioception.
source: As expected, oviposition decisions require multiple sensory modalities, such as visual, olfactory, gustatory and proprioception (Yang et al., 2008; Joseph et al., 2009; Schwartz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies characterizing sensory inputs to oviposition (Yang et al., 2008; Joseph et al., 2009; Schwartz et al., 2012).

claim: A previously considered female-only decision (oviposition) can be modulated by a male-deposited pheromone.
source: Our study shows that a previously considered female-only decision can in fact be modulated by a male-deposited pheromone.
evidence: This conclusion is based on data showing that male-deposited 9-tricosene guides female oviposition decisions.

claim: 9-tricosene could be a mechanism used by Drosophila males to increase the likelihood that their progeny will be laid in an optimal location.
source: Since 9-tricosene is enriched only upon food-odor stimulation, and acts to aggregate animals and increase courtship (Lin and Potter, unpublished observations), it could be a mechanism used by Drosophila males to increase the likelihood that their progeny will be laid in an optimal location.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed properties of 9-tricosene (food-odor induced, guides oviposition, increases courtship).

claim: In addition to 'mother-knows-best', 'father' may have co-opted a female's olfactory system to influence egg-laying decisions for maximizing progeny survival.
source: Thus, in addition to 'mother-knows-best', this suggest that 'father' may have co-opted a female's olfactory system in order to influence an egg-laying decision for maximizing progeny survival.
evidence: This is speculation based on the finding that male-deposited pheromone influences female oviposition decisions.

claim: 9-tricosene is a specific activator of Or7a, but Or7a is not activated only by 9-tricosene.
source: 9-Tricosene is a specific activator of Or7a, but Or7a is not activated only by 9-tricosene.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data showing 9-tricosene specifically activates Or7a, combined with previous knowledge that Or7a responds to many odorants.

claim: There is a strong positive correlation between the specificity of Or7a activation and oviposition-guidance.
source: Our behavioral experiments suggest a strong positive correlation with the specificity of Or7a activation and oviposition-guidance.
evidence: Behavioral data show that more specific Or7a agonists (9-tricosene, 1-propanol) elicit stronger oviposition preferences than less specific agonists (benzaldehyde, 1-butanol) (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).

claim: Activation of the Or7a olfactory receptor neuron can strongly influence egg-laying decisions.
source: This suggests that activation of the Or7a olfactory receptor neuron can strongly influence egg-laying decisions.
evidence: This conclusion is based on behavioral data showing Or7a agonists guide oviposition and optogenetic activation of Or7a neurons is sufficient to guide oviposition.

claim: 9-tricosene may have a specific influence on oviposition decisions due to its specific activation of Or7a.
source: 9-Tricosense may therefore have a specific influence on oviposition decisions due to its specific activation of Or7a.
evidence: This inference is based on the observation that 9-tricosene specifically activates Or7a and that Or7a activation influences oviposition.

claim: Or7a olfactory neurons join a growing list of olfactory neurons found to mediate specific olfactory behaviors.
source: Or7a olfactory neurons join a growing list of olfactory neurons found to mediate specific olfactory behaviors like oviposition-site selection (Dweck et al., 2013, 2015b), aversion (Suh et al., 2004; Ai et al., 2010; Stensmyr et al., 2012), courtship (Kurtovic et al., 2007), and attraction (Semmelhack and Wang, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies identifying specific olfactory neurons mediating specific behaviors.

claim: Odorants besides 9-tricosene that stimulate Or7a neurons will activate additional olfactory receptor neurons that may function to mask or modulate Or7a-mediated egg-laying behaviors.
source: Odorants besides 9-tricosene that stimulate Or7a neurons will activate additional olfactory receptor neurons that may function to mask or modulate Or7a-mediated egg-laying behaviors.
evidence: This inference is based on the observation that less specific Or7a agonists (which activate other receptors) show reduced oviposition guidance compared to specific agonists.

claim: Olfactory systems function to make sense of a complex environment by assigning biological weights and values to different olfactory neuron activity patterns that together influence a behavioral choice.
source: This likely reflects how olfactory systems function to make sense of a complex environment, by assigning biological weights and values to different olfactory neuron activity patterns that together influence a behavioral choice.
evidence: This is a general principle inferred from the observed data on how Or7a and other olfactory neurons influence behavior.

claim: Food odors and pheromone signals project to non-overlapping divisions in higher brain regions in Drosophila.
source: Food odors and pheromone signals have been shown to project to non-overlapping divisions in higher brain regions in Drosophila, suggesting that distinct brain divisions may be involved in mediating different biological functions (Jefferis et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on olfactory projection patterns (Jefferis et al., 2007).

claim: Basiconic Or7a neurons are responsible for 9-tricosene and E2-hexenal guided oviposition decisions.
source: We demonstrate that basiconic Or7a neurons are responsible for 9-tricosene and E2-hexenal guided oviposition decisions (Figure 6C,D,7C,7D).
evidence: Behavioral data show that Or7a mutants and Or7a neuron-ablated flies lack oviposition preference for both 9-tricosene and E2-hexenal (Figures 6C,D and 7C,D).

claim: Flies prefer citrus fruit as oviposition substrates as detected by Or19a+ olfactory neurons.
source: Recently, it was found that flies preferred citrus fruit as oviposition substrates as detected by Or19a + olfactory neurons (Dweck et al., 2013), and also preferred to oviposit on substrates containing ethylphenols as detected by Or71a + olfactory neurons (Dweck et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies identifying Or19a and Or71a roles in oviposition (Dweck et al., 2013, 2015b).

claim: Flies prefer to oviposit on substrates containing ethylphenols as detected by Or71a+ olfactory neurons.
source: Recently, it was found that flies preferred citrus fruit as oviposition substrates as detected by Or19a + olfactory neurons (Dweck et al., 2013), and also preferred to oviposit on substrates containing ethylphenols as detected by Or71a + olfactory neurons (Dweck et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on Or71a and oviposition (Dweck et al., 2015b).

claim: The Or7a DL5, Or19a DC1, and Or71a VC2 projection neurons share highly similar axonal projection patterns in the lateral horn that are distinct from previously described food and pheromone regions.
source: Interestingly, the Or7a DL5, Or19a DC1, and Or71a VC2 projection neurons share highly similar axonal projection patterns in the lateral horn that are distinct from previously described food and pheromone regions (Jefferis et al., 2007; Ronderos et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies characterizing projection neuron anatomy (Jefferis et al., 2007; Ronderos et al., 2014).

claim: Oviposition site-selection might be strongly guided by a dedicated olfactory processing brain center.
source: This suggests that oviposition site-selection might be strongly guided by a dedicated olfactory processing brain center.
evidence: This inference is based on the observation that multiple olfactory neurons guiding oviposition (Or7a, Or19a, Or71a) project to similar regions in the lateral horn.
